content: The emphasis is on creating software, workflows, and infrastructure that make data processing, analysis, and sharing reliable and repeatable. By providing versioned datasets, pipelines, and tooling (for example for neuroimaging and behavioral measurements), the aim is to reduce technical barriers, minimize errors, and help researchers reproduce results and reuse resources across projects.
title: Build tools for reproducible, shareable science

content:
The Center for Open Neuroscience brings open practices into the everyday work of neuroscience. We build, connect, test, document, and share the tools and infrastructure that help researchers work transparently and reproducibly.
Objectives # Promote open science through shared data and collaboration (Long-term goal) Connect tools, standards, and communities (Long-term goal) Preserve research artifacts (Long-term goal) Self-hosted research IT infrastructure (Long-term goal) Turn research ideas into working tools (Long-term goal) Understand brain function during everyday experiences (Long-term goal) Build tools for reproducible, shareable science (Long-term goal) Our principles #Open source #Open source supports collaboration at scale and makes scientific work easier to inspect, verify, and reproduce. CON also helps scientific developers make informed choices about licensing and sustainable development practices.
Re-use and integration #Research communities already produce powerful software and valuable data. Before inventing another solution, we look for ways to improve, connect, and reuse what exists.
Dissemination #Scientific projects rarely have dedicated resources for promotion or reliable distribution. We help share software, data, and documentation while paying attention to intellectual property and due acknowledgment.
Quality assurance #Research software deserves the same care as other scientific instruments. We work on unit, regression, integration, and validity testing so that reproducible workflows also produce trustworthy results.
Convenience #Open resources can have broad impact only when people can obtain and use them. We work to make software and data accessible without hiding their provenance or the complexity needed to manage them responsibly.
Community #Neuroscience spans many disciplines, yet projects can still develop in isolation. CON participates in cross-community initiatives and helps build bridges among research groups.
Explore CON projects or meet the people behind them.
Background reading # Open and reproducible neuroimaging: from study inception to publication Four aspects to make science open “by design” and not as an after-thought Open is not enough. Let’s take the next step: an integrated, community-driven computing platform for neuroscience Engage #Contribute #CON is an open community. You are welcome to build, document, test, teach, or use any of our projects, whether or not you are looking for a formal position.
Start with the DataLad project, browse the full catalogue, or contact the team to discuss where your experience could help.
Promote #Scientific software projects rarely have dedicated resources for community outreach. The following CON materials are available for exhibits, bulletin boards, teaching, and conversations about open neuroscience. Follow each pamphlet image to its printable PDF where available.
Pamphlet collation # A single-page collection of QR codes for the pamphlets below.
Python in electrophysiology # A double-sided introduction to Python-based projects for electrophysiology. The artwork sources are public.
Python in neuroimaging # A double-sided introduction to Python-based projects for neuroimaging. The artwork sources are public.
Debian and NeuroDebian # This pamphlet introduces Debian and the NeuroDebian project. Its artwork sources are public.
git-annex and DataLad # A double-sided introduction to DataLad and git-annex. The artwork sources are public.
BIDS # This pamphlet introduces the Brain Imaging Data Structure, a standardized layout that helps researchers reuse methods and share neuroimaging data.
Support #CON has received institutional and grant support from the organizations below. These acknowledgments describe past support, not current award periods.
Center for Cognitive Neuroscience # National Science Foundation # National Institutes of Health # Support helps CON maintain open software, data services, documentation, and community infrastructure. Contact the team to discuss sponsorship or other forms of support.

content:
con/fscacher is a Python library providing a persistent, file-content-aware memoization cache. Functions decorated with @cache.memoize_path are re-executed only when the fingerprint (timestamps + size) of their file arguments changes — making it easy to cache expensive operations on large file trees without stale results. It is used internally by the DANDI client and other CON tools.

con/tributors is a Python library and GitHub Action to automate maintenance of contributor attribution files. It updates all-contributors, Zenodo metadata (.zenodo.json), and CodeMeta (codemeta.json) files in one go, using a shared .tributors cache that maps GitHub logins to ORCID iDs and other persistent identifiers — so that contributor records stay consistent and up-to-date across all metadata files with a single command. content:
STAMPED is a set of seven principles, Self-containment, Tracking, Actionability, Modularity, Portability, Ephemerality, and Distributability, for building research objects that others can trust, rerun, and build upon. Each principle is a spectrum from a practical minimum to an aspirational ideal, so adoption can be incremental and start from existing practice. STAMPED grew out of YODA and comes with an interactive checklist and worked examples.

content:
Develop and test software, data standards, and analysis workflows that help researchers put new methods into practice.
New methods become useful when other researchers can run them, inspect them, and build on them. We work with research communities to develop and test software, ways of organizing data, and analysis steps that work together. This helps people use research methods in their own studies.
title: Turn research ideas into working tools

content:
Develop and test better ways to analyse brain activity and behaviour during rich experiences, such as watching a film.
Films combine images, sound, and events that unfold over time. Understanding the brain’s responses takes methods that can handle these details together. We develop and test ways to make that analysis more reliable and practical, so researchers can learn more from the same recordings. This builds on Psychoinformatics’ objective for naturalistic studies.
title: Understand brain function during everyday experiences
